subject: Culture
title: Mountain Worship
description: A fast breakdown of Mountain Worship for builders.

hook.text: Mount Kailash in Tibet has never been climbed. No government allows it. Four religions consider it sacred.

buildup.text: Mountains are sacred across cultures: Olympus for Greeks, Sinai for Jews, Fuji for Shinto practitioners.

discovery.text: Height creates awe, and awe triggers the brain's 'small self' response—feeling tiny beside something vast.

twist.text: When Edmund Hillary summited Everest in 1953, Sherpas were conflicted. Climbing Chomolungma was touching a goddess.

climax.text: Tourism is desecrating mountains that were protected by reverence. Everest now has a garbage problem.

punchline.text: We stopped worshipping mountains and started trashing them.

quiz.question: How many religions consider Mount Kailash sacred?

details.summary: Mountains are sacred across cultures — Mount Sinai in Judaism and Christianity, Mount Kailash in Hinduism and Buddhism, Mount Fuji in Shinto. Their height, danger, and cloud-shrouded peaks make mountains natural candidates for where Earth meets heaven and humans encounter the divine.
details.whyItMatters: Mountain worship reveals a universal human instinct to locate the divine at heights. From every continent, cultures independently concluded that gods dwell above — and mountains are the closest humans can climb.
takeaways: Mount Kailash is sacred to four religions and has never been climbed
Mount Sinai is where Moses received the Ten Commandments
Mountain pilgrimage exists independently in Asian, European, and American cultures

faq.question: Why are mountains universally considered sacred?
faq.answer: Mountains combine physical impressiveness (height, danger, permanence), atmospheric phenomena (cloud caps, lightning, unusual light), and psychological symbolism (ascent as spiritual progress, summit as divine encounter).

faq.question: Why has Mount Kailash never been climbed?
faq.answer: Mount Kailash (6,638m) in Tibet is sacred to Hinduism, Buddhism, Jainism, and Bon. China, which controls the area, has not issued climbing permits out of respect for religious sentiment. When a climbing expedition was proposed in 2001, international outcry from religious communities halted it.
